newsitem.title: INDONESIA: S.E. Asia currencies hit again after rupiah float.
newsitem.headline: S.E. Asia currencies hit again after rupiah float.

text.p: The Indonesian rupiah dropped to a new low on Friday after its effective float and brought other Southeast Asian currencies down with it.
The rupiah quickly lost an early firmness and fell to a record low of 2,890 to the dollar as overnight rates dropped back to 30 percent from an early high of 125 percent.
At 0430 GMT, the rupiah was at 2,875/80 at against its opening at 2,770/90.

Overnight rates shot up due to the central bank's tight short-term monetary policy and the maturity on Friday of its intervention on Wednesday, when it sold about $500 million to defend the rupiah from a speculative onslaught.
"People are just toying around with the rupiah and it's affecting the other currencies as well. We're looking for 3,000 on dollar/rupiah at some point," a Singapore-based dealer said.
On Thursday, Bank Indonesia gave up its system of managing the exchange rate through the use of an intervention band.
Analysts hailed the move as a welcome response to currency and economic turmoil in the region, which has highlighted the need for greater exchange rate flexibility.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) welcomed the float, saying it would allow the Indonesian economy to continue a recent impressive performance.

"In present circumstances, a floating exchange rate will enhance the effectiveness of macroeconomic policies aimed at sustaining high rates of growth with financial stability," said acting IMF managing director Stanley Fischer.
Dealers said the rupiah's decline pushed the Singapore dollar to a 37-month low of 1.5220 to the U.S. dollar.
"Nowadays, the regional currencies are traded as a group so if any one of them is being attacked, the rest of them will be pushed down as well," the Singapore dealer said.
Speculation of intervention by Singapore monetary authorities helped the Singapore dollar recover from its lows, but dealers said it was still heading for 1.53.
The rupiah fall also hit the Malaysian ringgit, which fell 2.7900/30 to the dollar against 2.7650/700 late on Thursday.
Dealers said the worst was not over for the ringgit given weak sentiment and the volatility in regional currencies.
They said the risk to the 2.80 level and beyond remained intact though the dollar was expected to face strong resistance at 2.7950.

The Thai baht eased on continued commercial demand for the dollar, but activity was relatively muted as the market awaited an official announcement of a reported cabinet reshuffle, even though it was expected to have only a limited impact.
The baht was at 31.60/31.70 to the dollar in the domestic market against 31.50/31.60 late on Thursday. It was at 31.50/60 in offshore markets.
The Philippine peso fell to 29.71/81 to the dollar at 0430 GMT against its previous close at 29.49.

Manila traders said the central bank continued to quote offer rates for the dollar at 10 centavos above the best market offer. The peso was expected to test a record low of 30, but dealers said some support was likely at 29.85.
The Taiwan dollar's decline was cushioned by central bank sales of the U.S. dollar near T$28.727 in the face of persistent demand from importers.
The Taiwan dollar was at T$28.726/727 against Thursday's T$28.725 close.
